ch05.card: Part 4 of 10. Asking the calculator for help.
ch05.s01.c1: Why hand sums to a pocket calculator? This part is about two pieces: the call writer, which writes a request slip, and the calculator, which answers it.
ch05.s01.c2: One rule, from the project rules on Oct 7. Hand-written code may run only as an outside tool that the model chooses to call.
ch05.s02.c1: Here's the catch. Code adds two numbers exactly, every time. That is our reasoning, not a measured result.
ch05.s02.c2: A learned network has to learn each sum from practice.
ch05.s02.c3: So the model writes its sum on a text slip, with made-up numbers here, and hands it to a calculator.
ch05.s03.c1: After a round, which is one lap of the thinker, the call writer reads the thinker's first control vector, a list of numbers. Think of a team leader glancing at the whiteboard.
ch05.s03.c2: Then it picks one of nine choices. Either no call, or one of the eight operations. The shading is only decoration.
ch05.s04.c1: Eight operations, with made-up numbers 12 and 5. We worked out each result by hand. A question mark means the call cannot run. Add gives 17. Sub, first minus second, gives 7. Mul gives 60. Guess div? Divide only works if exact, so a question mark. Mod, the left over, is 2. Min is 5. Max is 12. And cmp says 1 if the first is bigger, 0 if the same, negative 1 if less. Here, 1.
ch05.s05.c1: How does a number get onto the slip? Tom has 12 apples, a made-up example. A learned pointer lands on the last digit, the 2.
ch05.s05.c2: The copy then steps one letter left and copies the 1. Numbers get written last digit first.
ch05.s05.c3: A learned stop head says when to stop. Like a finger sliding along the page, then lifting.
ch05.s05.c4: How often does it use this trick? Across all six separate copies (T1SDR), it was used for 98% of written operands and 91.5% of answers.
ch05.s05.c5: Careful: copied here means the trick was used, not that the copy was right.
ch05.s06.c1: What if a number is in neither the question nor a reply? The call writer builds it one digit at a time, last digit first. Picture it filling one box per digit.
ch05.s06.c2: Those boxes are called cells. Tested copies had 11 cells. The never-run build of the finished design has 21, last digit first. The code flips the text.
ch05.s07.c1: And the calculator? Plain Python code. It has 0 learned numbers.
ch05.s07.c2: It reads a call as text, made-up numbers here, and writes the reply as text. A call it cannot run gets a question mark.
ch05.s08.c1: Now watch the slip travel. Take our made-up Tom example. After round 2 the call writer writes sub 12, 5, and the calculator replies.
ch05.s08.c2: The reply, sub 12, 5 equals 7, is read as new text by the reader's letter window, which sees nearby letters. Then it is added to the notes.
ch05.s08.c3: The question is not read again. After round 3 the call writer writes add 7, 3, and the calculator replies 10. Tom's answer.
ch05.s09.c1: When can a call happen? In the tested design, the first call follows round 2.
ch05.s09.c2: Call k follows round k plus 1, up to call 7 after round 8. Here k just stands for the call's number.
ch05.s09.c3: The tested copies ran 8 rounds. In the built learned-stop code, rounds 9 to 32 cannot call. That code has never run.
ch05.s10.c1: The project owner chose any time for when a call may follow.
ch05.s10.c2: The finished design's first build lets a call follow any round from 2 to 32. Built, never run.
ch05.s10.c3: The tape, the list of calls and replies so far, holds 16 calls.
ch05.s10.c4: In training, 1 row in 4 gets 0, 1 or 2 extra thinking rounds before each call.
ch05.s11.c1: Is anything still hand-made? Yes. Some parts are ordinary code a person wrote. Four are shown here in brown boxes.
ch05.s11.c2: The operation name comes from a fixed list of 8, so a new tool could not be called yet.
ch05.s11.c3: The second build writes the whole call as letters, operation name included.
ch05.s11.c4: It is built as code and has never run. So it has no results yet.
ch05.s12.c1: Does keeping it outside help? Evidence time. Each copy starts from its own random start.
ch05.s12.c2: The calculator-outside model, T1SDR, was compared with a similar calculator-inside model, B2.
ch05.s12.c3: On 6,040 questions kept aside, pooled over 5, T1SDR minus B2 is plus 0.62. The likely range runs from minus 0.23 to plus 1.46.
ch05.s12.c4: No copy fell over 1.0 below B2. The range includes 0, so there is no clear difference.
ch05.s12b.c1: On Chain-5, 1,000 multi-step questions, the calculator outside scored 99.6 to 99.8, mean 99.72. Inside, it scored 99.4 to 99.7.
ch05.s12b.c2: Now switch the calculator off. The 2,085 questions that need it score 0.0. So those answers depend on it.
ch05.s13.c1: Does the model really use it, or just look busy? A trap: add and sub are secretly swapped inside the calculator. The answer should follow the new reply.
ch05.s13.c2: Pass line: 99% or more of counted rows follow the swap. Rows with two possible sources don't count.
ch05.s13.c3: Five copies scored 99.28 to 99.87, all at 99 or more.
ch05.s13.c4: The run's own first reading was 97.1 to 97.6. Its scoring rule was then corrected, after the misses were studied.
ch05.s13.c5: The sixth copy's saved model was lost, so it is not scored.
ch05.s14.c1: A second trap, the leak check. Swap in another question's thinking, then count answers still right, out of 100, on 1,360 questions.
ch05.s14.c2: The limit was set before the run: 5. Five of six copies read above it, 5.07 to 5.59.
ch05.s14.c3: B2, with the calculator inside, read 3.09 to 3.75 on the same check.
ch05.s14.c4: It failed the limit. The project owner cleared it on Oct 9. It is disclosed, not a clean pass.
ch05.s14.c5: Separate reading, zero rounds of thinking: one copy read 12.94, against 10.81 for B2.
ch05.s15.c1: What is solid? Tested: the calculator outside the model, at 3M, over six copies. The swap check ran on five, and the owner cleared the leak check.
ch05.s15.c2: Never run together: the borrowed Gemma reader with the outside calculator.
ch05.s15.c3: Built, never run: calls at any round.
ch05.s15.c4: Remember: calls are text, replies are text, and a copy trick writes most numbers. Next question: who decides when the team is done? The stop switch.
